title: Perturbation, Not Provenance: Why Activation Steering Does Not Make a Robust Text Watermark

paper.title: Perturbation, Not Provenance: Why Activation Steering Does Not Make a Robust Text Watermark
paper.abstract:
Abstract Linear directions in the activation space of large language models causally and universally influence model behavior. This suggests that they might serve as a basis for a robust text watermark. The idea is to steer the generation along a specific semantic direction and then recover the mark by probing the activations of the re-encoded text.
We test this hypothesis by conducting a series of experiments. We vary the strength of the steering and use four different directions (formality, sentiment, complexity, and a random control) across two different model families. We also test two paraphrasing attacks: a sentence-level one and a stronger paragraph-level one.
The results show that activation-steering watermarks are outperformed by a standard logit-based watermark (KGW) in terms of detection accuracy. At a matched level of fluency (within 1.15 1.15 times the original text’s perplexity), KGW achieved an AUC of 0.81 0.81 against a sentence-level paraphraser, while the best steering direction only reached 0.65 0.65 . A stronger paragraph-level paraphraser lowered both ( 0.65 0.65 for KGW and 0.59 0.59 for steering), narrowing the gap but not reversing it. On Qwen, it left the two indistinguishable but at near-chance levels for both. We further showed that the detectability provided by steering was not semantic: a random direction was just as detectable as a meaningful one. The signal was independent of which layer was probed and whether a surface feature control was used. We conclude that, in this case, semantic activation does not encode a localized, recoverable semantic mark, but rather a global, content-independent shift that can only be strongly detected when the text is degraded.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text watermarking is a process of embedding a detectable signal into machine-generated text, allowing a third party with a specific key to later verify the text’s authenticity. A key aspect of watermarking is its resistance to paraphrasing, meaning that an adversary attempting to rewrite the text should not be able to easily remove the watermark. Watermarks based on logit functions, such as KGW ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) , bias token sampling towards a pseudo-random “green list”. On the other hand, there are semantic watermarks, like SemStamp ( Hou et al., 2024a ) , which target paraphrasing resistance by operating in the space of sentence embeddings. A natural and previously unexplored alternative is to embed a watermark inside the forward pass of the model. Recent work has shown that linear directions in the residual stream can causally steer the behavior of the model and generalize across different contexts. ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2024 ) . If a semantic direction leaves a trace that survives paraphrasing because new sentences preserve meaning even when they rewrite tokens, then we could: (i) steer generation along a secret semantic direction and (ii) detect the watermark by re-encoding the candidate text through the base model and probing its activations. Such a watermark would be architecturally different from logit- and embedding-space methods and might inherit the robustness of the underlying semantic representation to paraphrasing. We tested this hypothesis and reported a negative result. Our main contributions are: 1. We formalize and implement an activation-steering watermark and evaluate it against KGW on a detection-versus-fluency frontier, under both a sentence-level and a paragraph-level paraphrase attack, across steering strengths spanning fluent to degraded generation. 2. We show that the steering watermark is Pareto-dominated: at matched deployable fluency, it is never more detectable than KGW, and only reaches comparable detectability by inflating the perplexity by several-fold. 3. We demonstrate that its detectability is not semantic via three controls: a random steering direction matches meaningful ones, the signal is layer-invariant, and it cannot be explained by surface text statistics. We release data and code for further usage 1 1 1 https://github.com/A1exRey/Steering-Text-Watermarking .

sections.heading: Logit-based watermarks.
sections.text: KGW ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) and successors ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) partition the vocabulary and bias sampling; detection is a statistical test over token counts. These methods are known to degrade under paraphrase, motivating semantic approaches.

sections.heading: Semantic / paraphrase-robust watermarks.
sections.text: SemStamp ( Hou et al., 2024a ) and its variants ( Hou et al., 2024b ) operate in sentence-embedding space via rejection sampling to survive paraphrase. Our method differs by intervening in the residual stream; we find this confers no robustness advantage over the logit baseline at matched fluency.

sections.heading: Activation steering.
sections.text: Linear directions in activation space causally and generalizably affect model behavior ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2024 ) , which motivated the watermarking hypothesis we test. Our negative result delimits that promise: such directions do not yield a localized, recoverable semantic channel that survives paraphrase. Concurrent work, SLAM ( Harel-Canada and Sahai, 2026 ) , instantiates an activation-injection watermark using sparse-autoencoder structural directions (voice, tense, clause order) on Gemma-2. Our results delimit this specific case – the directions that transmit are behavioral and therefore collide with natural text. Steered structure that is not lexically anchored is what a paraphrasing tool removes. We test a sentence-level paraphrasing tool only, so we do not claim to overcome structural marks in SLAM; rather, we describe the secrecy-robustness tension that any such system must navigate.

sections.heading: Detection.
sections.text: The verifier re-encodes candidate text through the unmodified base model, mean-pools the layer- ℓ \ell activations over non-padding positions, and trains a regularized logistic probe to separate steered from unsteered text. We report detection as the cross-validated ROC-AUC of this probe (pooled across generation seeds).

sections.heading: Directions.
sections.text: We extract steering directions by mean-difference of pooled activations over contrastive text pairs ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) generated by a larger model of the same family: formality (formal vs. informal), sentiment (positive vs. negative), and complexity (complex vs. simple). As a control we use a random unit direction orthogonalized against formality. If steering encodes a semantic mark, the meaningful directions should be detectable and the random one should not.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against KGW ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) as implemented in, sweeping its logit bias δ \delta . KGW is detected with with its native z z -score test, not the activation probe. For paraphrasing we use two attackers. The first rewrites every generation sentence-by-sentence with a Pegasus ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . Because a sentence-level paraphraser is not able to reorder or merge material across sentence boundaries, we also use DIPPER ( Krishna et al., 2023 ) , a 11 ​ B 11B paragraph-level paraphraser that rewrites in few sentence windows.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and Qwen3-1.7B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) as generators, with the 8B model of each family used only to synthesize contrastive pairs.

sections.heading: Prompts and generation.
sections.text: We sample 200 200 Alpaca instruction prompts and generate with temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p p 0.9 0.9 and 150 150 max new tokens. Every operating point is generated under 3 3 seeds ( 600 600 generations per class).

sections.heading: Steering grid.
sections.text: The norm-relative fraction α \alpha is swept per model over a grid chosen by calibration to span fluent-but-changed to degraded generation ( α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} ). Because all figures plot detection against measured perplexity rather than against α \alpha , per-model grids remain directly comparable in fluency space.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: In both frontier figures (Figures 1 and 2 ) and in Table 1 , the y y -axis is post-paraphrase detection AUC; we report symmetric AUC ( max ⁡ ( AUC , 1 − AUC ) \max(\text{AUC},1{-}\text{AUC}) ) so a key-aware verifier’s separability is never under-counted. For the x x -axis we use a two-sided distortion d = | log ⁡ ( ppl steered / ppl unsteered ) | d=\lvert\log(\text{ppl}_{\text{steered}}/\text{ppl}_{\text{unsteered}})\rvert , the absolute log of the perplexity ratio under the base model. A one-sided "fluency cost" (perplexity ratio) is not adequate here because, on Qwen, several steering directions lower perplexity relative to the unsteered baseline, we analyze this in Results section.

sections.heading: A stronger attacker narrows the gap.
sections.text: DIPPER is much more damaging to KGW than Pegasus. When the attack is turned on, KGW loses an average of 0.15 0.15 AUC on Llama and 0.11 0.11 AUC on Qwen over its four different bias settings, while the four α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 points lose only 0.01 0.01 AUC, an order of magnitude less on both. This is expected, as KGW is more susceptible to the attack than the other models. A paragraph-level rewriter disrupts the token-level green list, whereas a probe on mean-pooled activations reads a global perturbation that partly survives rewording. On Llama, the gap therefore falls from 0.16 0.16 AUC under Pegasus to 0.06 0.06 under DIPPER, so Pegasus alone is an artifact of a weak attacker. On Qwen, the ordering does not survive: the best in-band steering point (sentiment, α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 )) reaches 0.587 0.587 against KGW’s 0.557 0.557 , a difference of − 0.03 -0.03 with interval [ − 0.07 , + 0.01 ] [-0.07,+0.01] . Under the stronger attack, the two are statistically indistinguishable on Qwen, and we do not claim KGW wins there. However, Qwen is the model on which KGW performs the worst, so the convergence reflects a decreasing baseline as well as an increasing steering curve. 0.587 0.587 is close enough to the chance level to be interpreted as neither method being effective here, rather than the steering curve succeeding. At the top of the steering grid, generation degenerates into empty or repetitive text whose perplexity ratio exceeds 10 × 10\times the unsteered baseline. We exclude these points from all figures and tables: they are not deployable watermarks but destroyed text.

sections.heading: Steering can reduce perplexity
sections.text: On Qwen3-1.7B several steering directions produce a perplexity ratio below 1 1 : steered generations are more probable under the base model than unsteered ones (formality and complexity at α ≤ 0.4 \alpha\leq 0.4 give 0.72 0.72 – 0.90 0.90 ). Steering towards "formal" or "complex" registers did not degrade fluency so much as homogenized output towards higher-probability, more generic phrasing. This gives us a methodological implication: detectability rises even as perplexity falls, so it cannot be a function of "fluency cost" alone. What the detector tracked was displacement from the base distribution in either direction, which was why our figures used the two-sided axis d d . Under it, the apparent "free detection" of these points resolved – they sat at moderate distortion ( d = 0.1 d=0.1 – 0.33 0.33 , not at zero cost. A second implication was that perplexity alone could not decide which points were deployable. Strong steering failed predominantly by repetition , and repeated tokens are highly predictable, so a collapsed completion has a low perplexity. On Qwen, this puts formality α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 at a 1.15 × 1.15\times ratio with 0.98 0.98 AUC – apparently a deployable watermark beating KGW – when one completion in ten has actually collapsed into a repetition loop. We therefore exclude operating points where more than 5% of completions are empty or have fewer than half their word 4-grams unique. On Qwen, this removes formality α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 and complexity α = 0.8 \alpha{=}0.8 ; on Llama, it removes nothing that the perplexity rule hadn’t already removed, so Table 1 . Detectability is achieved through degeneration, rather than a semantic marker.

sections.heading: 6 Ablation study
sections.text: If the steering encoded a semantic watermark, three predictions would hold: a meaningful direction would be more detectable than a random one, the signal would be strongest at the steered layer, and detection would not reduce to surface text statistics. However, the first two predictions fail outright, and the third is not refuted, but it is ineffective in the context that is relevant. At deployable fluency, there is no signal to explain surface statistics, because there is barely any signal at all. Where detection appears, it appears together with distortion, and it is available to a random direction as readily as it is to a meaningful one.

sections.heading: Random matches semantic.
sections.text: At matched steering strength the random control is among the most detectable directions, not the least. At α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 it reaches 0.86 0.86 AUC on Llama and 0.97 0.97 on Qwen, above formality ( 0.70 0.70 and 0.90 0.90 ), above complexity ( 0.59 0.59 and 0.68 0.68 ), and on Qwen above sentiment ( 0.64 0.64 ) as well; only Llama sentiment exceeds it. A direction carrying no semantic content is therefore no harder to recover than one carrying a concept. Direction identity does not even transfer between models. Sentiment is the most detectable direction on Llama at every steering strength and the least detectable on Qwen, though both were extracted by the same mean-difference procedure from the same contrastive template.

sections.heading: Layer invariance.
sections.text: The signal is flat across layers. We probe every other layer across the full depth of each model and compare detectability. Post-paraphrase AUC varies by at most 0.044 0.044 (Llama, 8 8 layers) and 0.054 0.054 (Qwen, 14 14 layers) across all probed layers, and the layer we actually steered is the probe-AUC maximum in none of the four directions on either model ( 0 / 4 0/4 each); the peaks land at scattered, unrelated layers. A watermark localized to the steered representation would peak there. Instead the signal is a global property of the generated text, detectable at any depth (Figures 3 and 4 ). Because we cover the whole stack rather than a few layers, this is not an undersampling artifact, and because the pattern is the same in both model families it is not a configuration or anomaly of one architecture. sections.heading: Surface statistics.
sections.text: At low, fluent steering ( α = 0.1 \alpha{=}0.1 ) neither probe separates the two sets. A probe trained only on shallow features (length, type–token ratio, punctuation rates) reaches 0.51 0.51 – 0.56 0.56 AUC, and the activation probe reaches 0.51 0.51 – 0.65 0.65 ; the two agree to within 0.02 0.02 for every direction on both models except sentiment on Llama, the single point where steering is detectable at deployable fluency. Matching the two sets on completion length leaves the activation AUC essentially unchanged, so length is not the confound either. The correct reading is not that a deep signal survives a surface control, but that at fluent steering there is almost no signal to begin with. At strong steering ( α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 ) both probes rise together, and the surface probe becomes accurate exactly where the text is most distorted ( 0.90 0.90 for the random direction on Qwen, 0.81 0.81 for sentiment on Llama). Surface detectability therefore rises in lockstep with distortion for the random control just as for the meaningful directions, which is the same conclusion the other two controls reach: detection tracks displacement from the base distribution, not content.

sections.heading: The sentiment exception.
sections.text: Sentiment is the one direction that becomes strongly detectable at modest perplexity on Llama (AUC 0.89 0.89 at 1.32 × 1.32\times ). It is, however, also layer-invariant: heavy sentiment steering makes the entire text conspicuously more positive, a global shift detectable at any layer rather than a localized mark. Nor does it replicate—on Qwen the same direction is the weakest of the four at every steering strength, reaching only 0.77 0.77 even at α = 0.8 \alpha{=}0.8 . The exception is a property of one direction in one model, and it illustrates the mechanism rather than contradicting it.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Semantic activation-steering watermarks are an interesting idea, but they do not work as expected. In the testing regime we used, which included two model families with approximately 1-2 billion parameters, a single steered layer at mid-depth, and both sentence-level and paragraph-level paraphrasing attacks, a logit watermark always dominated the model, regardless of the fluency cost. What we found was that what steering provided was non-semantic: a random direction matched meaningful ones, the signal was layer-invariant, and what survived a surface-statistics control was content-independent. Steering encoded a global perturbation that was only strongly detectable when it degraded text. We don’t claim that this rules out all activation-space watermarks – structural directions or larger models may behave differently – but it limits the semantic version of the idea, and we hope this saves others from taking a detour.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: We compare against a logit-based watermark (KGW) but not against a sentence-embedding watermark such as SemStamp ( Hou et al., 2024a ) . That is arguably the more natural comparison: like ours, and unlike KGW, it is designed for paraphrase robustness by operating on meaning rather than on tokens. We studied models with up to ≈ \approx 2B parameters and steered a single mid-depth layer in each model. Larger models, where steering directions may be cleaner and more linear, could potentially change the picture. However, this is beyond the scope of this study, and it is possible that our setup tests a less favorable case for the steering hypothesis than a large-scale study would, so the negative result is unlikely to change with scale. The concern about steering a single layer is also addressed by our design: the detector probes every layer and the signal is global rather than limited to the steered layer. Therefore, the claim does not depend on the specific layer being steered. Our detector is a deliberately strong key-aware probe; a more realistic key-blind detector would only lower steering detectability, reinforcing the negative result.

sections.heading: Why perplexity is insufficient.
sections.text: The frontier already discards points whose perplexity ratio exceeds 10 × 10\times as destroyed text. That rule cannot catch repetition, because a looping completion is highly predictable and therefore scores low perplexity. A point can be visibly destroyed and still sit in the deployable band. Qwen formality α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 is such a point: 1.15 × 1.15\times perplexity, 0.98 0.98 AUC, and completions such as " The singular and singularly singular singular singular and singularly singular and singularly singular and… "

sections.heading: This is not an artifact of self-scoring.
sections.text: Steering toward "formal" homogenizes text toward the steered model’s own high-probability phrasing, so one might suspect the ratio is depressed because the scorer is the model that was steered. It is not. Re-scoring every operating point under an independent Llama-3.1-8B judge places the same point at 1.13 × 1.13\times , against 1.15 × 1.15\times self-scored. Both scorers agree, because the effect is a property of the text: no perplexity based axis can rank output whose dominant failure mode is one that perplexity rewards.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.17810v1 [cs.CL] 13 Oct 2026 Perturbation, Not Provenance: Why Activation Steering Does Not Make a Robust Text Watermark Sergey Pletenev Affiliation: AIRI Affiliation: Skoltech Email: mailto:alex010rey@gmail.comalex010rey@gmail.com Abstract Linear directions in the activation space of large language models causally and universally influence model behavior. This suggests that they might serve as a basis for a robust text watermark. The idea is to steer the generation along a specific semantic direction and then recover the mark by probing the activations of the re-encoded text. We test this hypothesis by conducting a series of experiments. We vary the strength of the steering and use four different directions (formality, sentiment, complexity, and a random control) across two different model families. We also test two paraphrasing attacks: a sentence-level one and a stronger paragraph-level one. The results show that activation-steering watermarks are outperformed by a standard logit-based watermark (KGW) in terms of detection accuracy. At a matched level of fluency (within 1.15 1.15 times the original text’s perplexity), KGW achieved an AUC of 0.81 0.81 against a sentence-level paraphraser, while the best steering direction only reached 0.65 0.65 . A stronger paragraph-level paraphraser lowered both ( 0.65 0.65 for KGW and 0.59 0.59 for steering), narrowing the gap but not reversing it. On Qwen, it left the two indistinguishable but at near-chance levels for both. We further showed that the detectability provided by steering was not semantic: a random direction was just as detectable as a meaningful one. The signal was independent of which layer was probed and whether a surface feature control was used. We conclude that, in this case, semantic activation does not encode a localized, recoverable semantic mark, but rather a global, content-independent shift that can only be strongly detected when the text is degraded. 1 Introduction Text watermarking is a process of embedding a detectable signal into machine-generated text, allowing a third party with a specific key to later verify the text’s authenticity. A key aspect of watermarking is its resistance to paraphrasing, meaning that an adversary attempting to rewrite the text should not be able to easily remove the watermark. Watermarks based on logit functions, such as KGW ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) , bias token sampling towards a pseudo-random “green list”. On the other hand, there are semantic watermarks, like SemStamp ( Hou et al., 2024a ) , which target paraphrasing resistance by operating in the space of sentence embeddings. A natural and previously unexplored alternative is to embed a watermark inside the forward pass of the model. Recent work has shown that linear directions in the residual stream can causally steer the behavior of the model and generalize across different contexts. ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2024 ) . If a semantic direction leaves a trace that survives paraphrasing because new sentences preserve meaning even when they rewrite tokens, then we could: (i) steer generation along a secret semantic direction and (ii) detect the watermark by re-encoding the candidate text through the base model and probing its activations. Such a watermark would be architecturally different from logit- and embedding-space methods and might inherit the robustness of the underlying semantic representation to paraphrasing. We tested this hypothesis and reported a negative result. Our main contributions are: 1. We formalize and implement an activation-steering watermark and evaluate it against KGW on a detection-versus-fluency frontier, under both a sentence-level and a paragraph-level paraphrase attack, across steering strengths spanning fluent to degraded generation. 2. We show that the steering watermark is Pareto-dominated: at matched deployable fluency, it is never more detectable than KGW, and only reaches comparable detectability by inflating the perplexity by several-fold. 3. We demonstrate that its detectability is not semantic via three controls: a random steering direction matches meaningful ones, the signal is layer-invariant, and it cannot be explained by surface text statistics. We release data and code for further usage 1 1 1 https://github.com/A1exRey/Steering-Text-Watermarking . 2 Related Work Logit-based watermarks. KGW ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) and successors ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) partition the vocabulary and bias sampling; detection is a statistical test over token counts. These methods are known to degrade under paraphrase, motivating semantic approaches. Semantic / paraphrase-robust watermarks. SemStamp ( Hou et al., 2024a ) and its variants ( Hou et al., 2024b ) operate in sentence-embedding space via rejection sampling to survive paraphrase. Our method differs by intervening in the residual stream; we find this confers no robustness advantage over the logit baseline at matched fluency. Activation steering. Linear directions in activation space causally and generalizably affect model behavior ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2024 ) , which motivated the watermarking hypothesis we test. Our negative result delimits that promise: such directions do not yield a localized, recoverable semantic channel that survives paraphrase. Concurrent work, SLAM ( Harel-Canada and Sahai, 2026 ) , instantiates an activation-injection watermark using sparse-autoencoder structural directions (voice, tense, clause order) on Gemma-2. Our results delimit this specific case – the directions that transmit are behavioral and therefore collide with natural text. Steered structure that is not lexically anchored is what a paraphrasing tool removes. We test a sentence-level paraphrasing tool only, so we do not claim to overcome structural marks in SLAM; rather, we describe the secrecy-robustness tension that any such system must navigate. 3 Method Watermark by activation steering. Let h t ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ d h^{(\ell)}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the residual-stream activation at layer ℓ \ell and token position t t . Given a unit-norm steering direction v ∈ ℝ d v\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , we add, at every position during generation, h ~ t ( ℓ ) = h t ( ℓ ) + α ⁡ ∥ h t ( ℓ ) ∥ ​ v , \tilde{h}^{(\ell)}_{t}=h^{(\ell)}_{t}+\alpha\,\lVert h^{(\ell)}_{t}\rVert\,v, (1) where α \alpha is a norm-relative steering fraction. Scaling by ∥ h t ( ℓ ) ∥ \lVert h^{(\ell)}_{t}\rVert makes α \alpha comparable across models and layers whose residual norms differ by orders of magnitude (e.g. ≈ 10 2 \approx\!10^{2} for Llama-3.2-1B at ℓ = 8 \ell{=}8 versus ≈ × 10 3 \approx\!2.2\!\times\!10^{3} for Qwen3-1.7B at ℓ = 14 \ell{=}14 ); an absolute offset that steers one model is negligible or destructive for another. Detection. The verifier re-encodes candidate text through the unmodified base model, mean-pools the layer- ℓ \ell activations over non-padding positions, and trains a regularized logistic probe to separate steered from unsteered text. We report detection as the cross-validated ROC-AUC of this probe (pooled across generation seeds). Directions. We extract steering directions by mean-difference of pooled activations over contrastive text pairs ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) generated by a larger model of the same family: formality (formal vs. informal), sentiment (positive vs. negative), and complexity (complex vs. simple). As a control we use a random unit direction orthogonalized against formality. If steering encodes a semantic mark, the meaningful directions should be detectable and the random one should not. Baselines. We compare against KGW ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2023 ) as implemented in, sweeping its logit bias δ \delta . KGW is detected with with its native z z -score test, not the activation probe. For paraphrasing we use two attackers. The first rewrites every generation sentence-by-sentence with a Pegasus ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . Because a sentence-level paraphraser is not able to reorder or merge material across sentence boundaries, we also use DIPPER ( Krishna et al., 2023 ) , a 11 ​ B 11B paragraph-level paraphraser that rewrites in few sentence windows. 4 Experimental Setup Models. We use Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and Qwen3-1.7B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) as generators, with the 8B model of each family used only to synthesize contrastive pairs. Prompts and generation. We sample 200 200 Alpaca instruction prompts and generate with temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p p 0.9 0.9 and 150 150 max new tokens. Every operating point is generated under 3 3 seeds ( 600 600 generations per class). Steering grid. The norm-relative fraction α \alpha is swept per model over a grid chosen by calibration to span fluent-but-changed to degraded generation ( α ∈ { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.4 , 0.6 , 0.8 } \alpha\in\{0.1,0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\} ). Because all figures plot detection against measured perplexity rather than against α \alpha , per-model grids remain directly comparable in fluency space. Metrics. In both frontier figures (Figures 1 and 2 ) and in Table 1 , the y y -axis is post-paraphrase detection AUC; we report symmetric AUC ( max ⁡ ( AUC , 1 − AUC ) \max(\text{AUC},1{-}\text{AUC}) ) so a key-aware verifier’s separability is never under-counted. For the x x -axis we use a two-sided distortion d = | log ⁡ ( ppl steered / ppl unsteered ) | d=\lvert\log(\text{ppl}_{\text{steered}}/\text{ppl}_{\text{unsteered}})\rvert , the absolute log of the perplexity ratio under the base model. A one-sided "fluency cost" (perplexity ratio) is not adequate here because, on Qwen, several steering directions lower perplexity relative to the unsteered baseline, we analyze this in Results section. 5 Results Methods Ppl. d d AUC Peg {}_{\text{Peg}} AUC DIP {}_{\text{DIP}} Deployable regime ( ≤ 1.15 × \leq 1.15\times ppl) KGW ( δ = 3 \delta{=}3 ) 1.06 1.06 0.06 0.06 0.81 \mathbf{0.81} 0.65 \mathbf{0.65} sentiment ( α = 0.1 \alpha{=}0.1 ) 1.03 1.03 0.03 0.03 0.65 0.65 0.59 0.59 random ( α = 0.2 \alpha{=}0.2 ) 1.13 1.13 0.12 0.12 0.61 0.61 0.57 0.57 complexity ( α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 ) 1.03 1.03 0.03 0.03 0.59 0.59 0.55 0.55 formality ( α = 0.2 \alpha{=}0.2 ) 1.05 1.05 0.05 0.05 0.57 0.57 0.52 0.52 Steering’s high-detectability points formality ( α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 ) 1.73 1.73 0.55 0.55 0.91 0.91 0.83 0.83 sentiment ( α = 0.2 \alpha{=}0.2 ) 1.32 1.32 0.28 0.28 0.89 0.89 0.83 0.83 random ( α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 ) 1.98 1.98 0.68 0.68 0.86 0.86 0.78 0.78 Table 1: Llama-3.2-1B, best point per method within each case, under the Pegasus (Peg) and DIPPER (DIP) attacks. Ppl. is the ratio to unsteered and d = | log ⁡ ( ppl ratio ) | d=\lvert\log(\text{ppl ratio})\rvert Figure 1: Detection-versus-distortion frontier (Llama-3.2-1B) Figure 2: Detection-versus-distortion frontier (Qwen3-1.7B) Table 1 and Figures 1 and 2 show the main results. In the deployable case, KGW achieves 0.81 0.81 post-paraphrase AUC with a perplexity of 1.06 1.06 . No other approach comes close to this level of performance at comparable fluency. Sentiment achieves the best result with 0.65 0.65 AUC, and the remaining three approaches fall between 0.57 0.57 and 0.61 0.61 . Steering matches KGW’s best operating point ( 0.85 0.85 ) only from a perplexity of 1.16 1.16 upward. Non-sentiment approaches only perform well at 1.7 1.7 - 2 × 2\times , which corresponds to a noticeable degradation in text quality. The logit watermark dominates the activation-steering watermark across the frontier, except for one case: on Qwen, sentiment with α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 reaches 0.77 0.77 , which is higher than KGW’s best ( 0.71 0.71 ), but at a greater distortion ( d = 0.18 d=0.18 compared to 0.12 0.12 ). Because both detectors score the same unsteered negative set, their AUCs are correlated, so we bootstrap the difference directly, resampling whole prompts (each prompt contributes one generation per seed to each class) and recomputing both AUCs on every replicate. In the deployable band KGW exceeds the best steering direction by 0.16 0.16 AUC under Pegasus, and no replicate put the difference at or below zero. The curves do not overlap within their error bars anywhere in the low-distortion regime (Figure 1 ). A stronger attacker narrows the gap. DIPPER is much more damaging to KGW than Pegasus. When the attack is turned on, KGW loses an average of 0.15 0.15 AUC on Llama and 0.11 0.11 AUC on Qwen over its four different bias settings, while the four α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 points lose only 0.01 0.01 AUC, an order of magnitude less on both. This is expected, as KGW is more susceptible to the attack than the other models. A paragraph-level rewriter disrupts the token-level green list, whereas a probe on mean-pooled activations reads a global perturbation that partly survives rewording. On Llama, the gap therefore falls from 0.16 0.16 AUC under Pegasus to 0.06 0.06 under DIPPER, so Pegasus alone is an artifact of a weak attacker. On Qwen, the ordering does not survive: the best in-band steering point (sentiment, α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 )) reaches 0.587 0.587 against KGW’s 0.557 0.557 , a difference of − 0.03 -0.03 with interval [ − 0.07 , + 0.01 ] [-0.07,+0.01] . Under the stronger attack, the two are statistically indistinguishable on Qwen, and we do not claim KGW wins there. However, Qwen is the model on which KGW performs the worst, so the convergence reflects a decreasing baseline as well as an increasing steering curve. 0.587 0.587 is close enough to the chance level to be interpreted as neither method being effective here, rather than the steering curve succeeding. At the top of the steering grid, generation degenerates into empty or repetitive text whose perplexity ratio exceeds 10 × 10\times the unsteered baseline. We exclude these points from all figures and tables: they are not deployable watermarks but destroyed text. Steering can reduce perplexity On Qwen3-1.7B several steering directions produce a perplexity ratio below 1 1 : steered generations are more probable under the base model than unsteered ones (formality and complexity at α ≤ 0.4 \alpha\leq 0.4 give 0.72 0.72 – 0.90 0.90 ). Steering towards "formal" or "complex" registers did not degrade fluency so much as homogenized output towards higher-probability, more generic phrasing. This gives us a methodological implication: detectability rises even as perplexity falls, so it cannot be a function of "fluency cost" alone. What the detector tracked was displacement from the base distribution in either direction, which was why our figures used the two-sided axis d d . Under it, the apparent "free detection" of these points resolved – they sat at moderate distortion ( d = 0.1 d=0.1 – 0.33 0.33 , not at zero cost. A second implication was that perplexity alone could not decide which points were deployable. Strong steering failed predominantly by repetition , and repeated tokens are highly predictable, so a collapsed completion has a low perplexity. On Qwen, this puts formality α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 at a 1.15 × 1.15\times ratio with 0.98 0.98 AUC – apparently a deployable watermark beating KGW – when one completion in ten has actually collapsed into a repetition loop. We therefore exclude operating points where more than 5% of completions are empty or have fewer than half their word 4-grams unique. On Qwen, this removes formality α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 and complexity α = 0.8 \alpha{=}0.8 ; on Llama, it removes nothing that the perplexity rule hadn’t already removed, so Table 1 . Appendix A.2 gives the criterion, an independent cross-model check confirming the effect is not an artifact of self-scoring, and per-point collapse rates. Detectability is achieved through degeneration, rather than a semantic marker. 6 Ablation study If the steering encoded a semantic watermark, three predictions would hold: a meaningful direction would be more detectable than a random one, the signal would be strongest at the steered layer, and detection would not reduce to surface text statistics. However, the first two predictions fail outright, and the third is not refuted, but it is ineffective in the context that is relevant. At deployable fluency, there is no signal to explain surface statistics, because there is barely any signal at all. Where detection appears, it appears together with distortion, and it is available to a random direction as readily as it is to a meaningful one. Random matches semantic. At matched steering strength the random control is among the most detectable directions, not the least. At α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 it reaches 0.86 0.86 AUC on Llama and 0.97 0.97 on Qwen, above formality ( 0.70 0.70 and 0.90 0.90 ), above complexity ( 0.59 0.59 and 0.68 0.68 ), and on Qwen above sentiment ( 0.64 0.64 ) as well; only Llama sentiment exceeds it. A direction carrying no semantic content is therefore no harder to recover than one carrying a concept. Direction identity does not even transfer between models. Sentiment is the most detectable direction on Llama at every steering strength and the least detectable on Qwen, though both were extracted by the same mean-difference procedure from the same contrastive template. Layer invariance. The signal is flat across layers. We probe every other layer across the full depth of each model and compare detectability. Post-paraphrase AUC varies by at most 0.044 0.044 (Llama, 8 8 layers) and 0.054 0.054 (Qwen, 14 14 layers) across all probed layers, and the layer we actually steered is the probe-AUC maximum in none of the four directions on either model ( 0 / 4 0/4 each); the peaks land at scattered, unrelated layers. A watermark localized to the steered representation would peak there. Instead the signal is a global property of the generated text, detectable at any depth (Figures 3 and 4 ). Because we cover the whole stack rather than a few layers, this is not an undersampling artifact, and because the pattern is the same in both model families it is not a configuration or anomaly of one architecture. Figure 3: Post-paraphrase detectability against probe layer on Llama-3.2-1B. Rings mark each direction’s peak layer; the dash-dotted line is the layer that was steered. "low" is α = 0.1 \alpha{=}0.1 and "strong" is α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 . Figure 4: Post-paraphrase detectability against probe layer on Qwen3-1.7B Surface statistics. At low, fluent steering ( α = 0.1 \alpha{=}0.1 ) neither probe separates the two sets. A probe trained only on shallow features (length, type–token ratio, punctuation rates) reaches 0.51 0.51 – 0.56 0.56 AUC, and the activation probe reaches 0.51 0.51 – 0.65 0.65 ; the two agree to within 0.02 0.02 for every direction on both models except sentiment on Llama, the single point where steering is detectable at deployable fluency. Matching the two sets on completion length leaves the activation AUC essentially unchanged, so length is not the confound either. The correct reading is not that a deep signal survives a surface control, but that at fluent steering there is almost no signal to begin with. At strong steering ( α = 0.4 \alpha{=}0.4 ) both probes rise together, and the surface probe becomes accurate exactly where the text is most distorted ( 0.90 0.90 for the random direction on Qwen, 0.81 0.81 for sentiment on Llama). Surface detectability therefore rises in lockstep with distortion for the random control just as for the meaningful directions, which is the same conclusion the other two controls reach: detection tracks displacement from the base distribution, not content. The sentiment exception. Sentiment is the one direction that becomes strongly detectable at modest perplexity on Llama (AUC 0.89 0.89 at 1.32 × 1.32\times ). It is, however, also layer-invariant: heavy sentiment steering makes the entire text conspicuously more positive, a global shift detectable at any layer rather than a localized mark. Nor does it replicate—on Qwen the same direction is the weakest of the four at every steering strength, reaching only 0.77 0.77 even at α = 0.8 \alpha{=}0.8 . The exception is a property of one direction in one model, and it illustrates the mechanism rather than contradicting it. 7 Conclusion Semantic activation-steering watermarks are an interesting idea, but they do not work as expected. In the testing regime we used, which included two model families with approximately 1-2 billion parameters, a single steered layer at mid-depth, and both sentence-level and paragraph-level paraphrasing attacks, a logit watermark always dominated the model, regardless of the fluency cost. What we found was that what steering provided was non-semantic: a random direction matched meaningful ones, the signal was layer-invariant, and what survived a surface-statistics control was content-independent. Steering encoded a global perturbation that was only strongly detectable when it degraded text. We don’t claim that this rules out all activation-space watermarks – structural directions or larger models may behave differently – but it limits the semantic version of the idea, and we hope this saves others from taking a detour. Limitations We compare against a logit-based watermark (KGW) but not against a sentence-embedding watermark such as SemStamp ( Hou et al., 2024a ) . That is arguably the more natural comparison: like ours, and unlike KGW, it is designed for paraphrase robustness by operating on meaning rather than on tokens. We studied models with up to ≈ \approx 2B parameters and steered a single mid-depth layer in each model. Larger models, where steering directions may be cleaner and more linear, could potentially change the picture. However, this is beyond the scope of this study, and it is possible that our setup tests a less favorable case for the steering hypothesis than a large-scale study would, so the negative result is unlikely to change with scale. The concern about steering a single layer is also addressed by our design: the detector probes every layer and the signal is global rather than limited to the steered layer. Therefore, the claim does not depend on the specific layer being steered. Our detector is a deliberately strong key-aware probe; a more realistic key-blind detector would only lower steering detectability, reinforcing the negative result. References Grattafiori et al. The frontier already discards points whose perplexity ratio exceeds 10 × 10\times as destroyed text. That rule cannot catch repetition, because a looping completion is highly predictable and therefore scores low perplexity. A point can be visibly destroyed and still sit in the deployable band. Qwen formality α = 0.6 \alpha{=}0.6 is such a point: 1.15 × 1.15\times perplexity, 0.98 0.98 AUC, and completions such as " The singular and singularly singular singular singular and singularly singular and singularly singular and… " This is not an artifact of self-scoring. Steering toward "formal" homogenizes text toward the steered model’s own high-probability phrasing, so one might suspect the ratio is depressed because the scorer is the model that was steered. It is not. Re-scoring every operating point under an independent Llama-3.1-8B judge places the same point at 1.13 × 1.13\times , against 1.15 × 1.15\times self-scored. Both scorers agree, because the effect is a property of the text: no perplexity based axis can rank output whose dominant failure mode is one that perplexity rewards.
